project.description: Aquaponic systems couple recirculating aquaculture with hydroponic crop production and depend on microbial communities to mediate nitrification, mineralisation of organic matter, and plant nutrient supply. The functional stability of these systems is therefore expected to rest on a small set of structurally important "keystone" taxa, yet whether such taxa exist in aquaponic microbiomes in the same form as in natural aquatic ecosystems has not been tested. The goal of this project is to apply three independent and mechanistically distinct keystone-screening approaches (leave-one-out PERMANOVA presence-impact analysis, co-occurrence network centrality, and LASSO regression on temporal turnover) to the same multi-compartment 16S rRNA gene amplicon dataset and to determine whether convergent keystone candidates emerge across coupled and decoupled hydraulic designs and across light and dark grow-bed regimes. Eighty-eight samples were collected from fish tanks, recirculating clarifiers, and hydroponic grow beds at the Auburn University research aquaponics facility across six dates between May 2024 and November 2024. The resulting microbiome reference is intended to support practical microbiome monitoring in aquaponics, to inform aquaponic system design and operation, and to contribute to the wider debate on whether the classical keystone concept developed for macro-ecological food webs translates to highly diverse, functionally redundant microbial communities.
